sm: The host opens by arguing that comedians like Bill Burr, George Carlin and Howard Stern lost their edge late in their careers, and says Dave Chappelle has followed the same path. He calls Chappelle overrated, says his career rested on a few jokes about white people, and says Chappelle's Show is remembered for about five sketches. He then turns to Chappelle's recent show at Madison Square Garden, where Chappelle said he felt better after Charlie Kirk was murdered. The host says there was no setup or punchline, and that Chappelle apparently made similar remarks at an earlier show in Toronto.

The host argues that saying you are happy someone died is not a joke, and that Louis C.K. is better at drawing comedy out of dark places. He says leaked footage shows the fuller context was worse, and that part of the Madison Square Garden crowd cheered while others seemed shocked. He rejects the defense that Chappelle is being brave or transgressive, saying the left already mocks Kirk constantly. He adds that a real belief delivered with no punchline is a statement, not comedy, and that backing away by saying it was a joke would be cowardice.

The host contrasts this with how Chappelle handled George Floyd, playing a clip in which Chappelle compared Floyd's death to an earthquake and spoke solemnly about it. He says Chappelle treated Floyd as a sacred cow. He disputes Chappelle's account, saying Floyd was a forty-six-year-old career criminal who died of an overdose, and that Derek Chauvin's knee was not on his neck for the full time. He also mocks Chappelle for saying this is a lot to unpack, and concludes that Chappelle does have subjects he will not touch.

The host asks why Chappelle is comfortable celebrating Kirk's death, and answers that Kirk was a white man who challenged narratives about Black victimhood. He responds to critics who compare Kirk jokes to jokes about George Floyd, Trayvon Martin and Minnesota lawmaker Melissa Hortman. He says Floyd and Martin were not murdered, that Floyd was a violent criminal who died of an overdose, and that mocking the way the left made Floyd a messiah is fair. He says Kirk broke no laws and was a good man who respected everyone, and says conservatives who accept Kirk jokes because of Floyd jokes should be disregarded.

The host says the point of mocking Kirk is that the left wants conservatives dead. He plays a clip from Jennifer Welch's podcast in which a guest jokes about digging Kirk up and doing it again, and says the hosts also claimed the shooter came from a white MAGA family. He says the left celebrates the killing while disavowing it, comparing that to the Weather Underground. He notes the shooter, Tyler Robinson, had a trans partner and wrote antifa messages on bullets. He then plays Scott Galloway calling Elon Musk a traitor who should be lined up against a wall, and joking that he defecated in his Tesla before selling it.

The host rejects the argument that leftists are only mocking Turning Point USA, saying the gloating began within seconds of the shooting. He says organizations can be criticized, but mocking a murder is different. He argues that anyone who gloats over a man being shot in the neck on camera has lost something human. He recalls that Chappelle was attacked on stage in 2022 with a replica gun holding a real knife blade, and that Kirk responded by criticizing the prosecutor, not mocking Chappelle. He then says Chappelle's career has been built on disdain for white people, and plays a 2004 NPR interview in which Chappelle explains how he does a white accent.

The host continues the NPR clip, in which Chappelle says his impressions are not malicious, and says white liberals love being mocked by celebrities. He says Chappelle's trans jokes were one of the few times he went after a real sacred cow. He admits conservatives gave Chappelle too much credit for them because every major institution had gone along with gender ideology. He plays a joke about LeBron James switching to the WNBA and scoring eight hundred and forty points a game, and calls it an actual joke, though a mild one.

The host says that joke had already been made countless times by conservatives, and that after the backlash Chappelle has been trying to win back the left, which is why he is now going after Kirk. He disputes the story that Chappelle walked away from a fifty million dollar deal on principle. He cites an account that Chappelle quit after a white man laughed loudly at a sketch about racial stereotypes, and says this shows Chappelle is anti-white. He concludes that Chappelle has always hated white people, which he says is the context for the Kirk comments, and that Chappelle is getting few laughs now.
